chandrayaan-3.story:
Chandrayaan-3 was an Indian Space Research Organisation mission that put the Vikram lander and the small Pragyan rover near the Moon's south pole, at about 69 degrees south, on 23 August 2023. India went there partly because studies show large amounts of ice in the region. It had lost an earlier lander, Chandrayaan-2, in 2019. The rover worked nearby until 3 September, about 11 days, when it was put to sleep ahead of the lunar night. Both machines remain at the site.

India calls the site Shiv Shakti point. The International Astronomical Union, the body that names features in space, accepted the name Statio Shiv Shakti in 2024. A name has no legal effect on who may use a place. Article II of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, bars claims to the Moon by any means. Article VIII leaves legal authority over the machines with India as the registering country.

Under Article IX, a later mission from another country must act with due regard for what others are doing there, and nothing in the treaty stops it landing nearby.
chandrayaan-3.why: Rover went to sleep on 3 September, about 11 days after landing, not 12.

slim.story:
SLIM, the Smart Lander for Investigating Moon, was a Japanese robot lander nicknamed the Moon Sniper. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) built it to show that a craft could land within 100 metres of its target. Apollo 11's landing area had been an oval 20 kilometres long. It found its way by recognising craters, with methods borrowed from face-recognition software, and it cost an expected 18 billion yen, about US$121.5 million.

It launched on 6 September 2023 and touched down near Shioli crater in the Sea of Nectar on 19 January 2024, making Japan the fifth country to land softly on the Moon. It came down on its side with its solar panels facing away from the Sun, so it ran briefly on its battery and was shut down by hand at 17:57 UTC the same day, to keep the battery from draining completely. It woke nine days later, when the sunlight moved round to the panels. It had not been designed to survive the bitter cold of the two-week lunar night, yet it did so three times, waking on 23 April 2024 after the third. It went silent in late May, and JAXA declared the mission over on 23 August 2024.

The silent spacecraft is still Japanese. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, says the country that registers a spacecraft keeps legal authority over it while it is in space or on another world, and that ownership does not change. The article sets no end date tied to the life of a mission. A dead lander is like a parked car in one respect, since nobody else may take it just because it has stopped working. The ground under it stays unclaimed.
slim.why: "Next day" is true only in Japan time; it was powered down at 17:57 UTC on 19 January, the day of landing, by hand to protect the battery.

for-all-moonkind.story:
For All Moonkind is a volunteer nonprofit, founded in 2017 by Tim and Michelle Hanlon, that works to protect the places on the Moon where people and machines have landed. Michelle Hanlon is a professor of air and space law at the University of Mississippi. The name plays on a phrase used twice in the Apollo programme. The plaque Apollo 11 left on the Moon spoke of peace for all mankind, and Gene Cernan used the same words as Apollo 17 left.

The worry behind the group is simple. Many countries and companies plan to return to the Moon, and a robot rover or a careless visitor could drive across Neil Armstrong's first footprints or damage the Apollo landers. On Earth a government protects such a place by declaring it a park or a heritage site. Machu Picchu in Peru, for example, is protected through its host country and the World Heritage Convention. The Moon has no host country. Article II of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the basic international agreement on space, says no nation can take any part of the Moon by claiming it, using it or occupying it. A country that declared a park around a landing site would be doing something very close to what the treaty forbids.

So the Hanlons have tried to build protection out of other materials. Their first aim was a proposal for the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space, the UN body that discusses space law and meets in Vienna, modelled on the World Heritage Convention. In December 2018 the UN General Assembly gave the group observer status on a provisional basis for three years, which lets it attend and speak at UN meetings without having a vote. It also approached companies directly, and the German firm PTScientists, then planning to send a rover to the Apollo 17 site, was the first to pledge support in public.

The second route was American law. In 2019 the group worked with the office of Senator Gary Peters on the One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act. The Senate passed it unanimously on 18 July 2019, the House passed it in December 2020, and it became law on 31 December 2020. Its reach is narrow. It does not fence off any ground. It requires companies working with NASA on Moon missions to agree to follow NASA's guidelines on keeping away from American landing sites, guidelines that could not otherwise be enforced. It works as a condition of a contract, so a company with no NASA contract is untouched. Hanlon herself wrote that the pool of affected companies is small, and that its importance is that it was the first law of any nation to recognise human heritage in space.

The third route is promises between governments. Section 9 of the Artemis Accords, a US-led set of principles first signed by eight countries in October 2020, commits signers to preserve historic landing sites, artefacts and spacecraft. It was the first time such heritage appeared in an agreement among several countries, and NASA counted 76 signing countries on 28 September 2026. In March 2021 the group released a free digital registry of historic landing sites, and in March 2023 it formed the Institute on Space Law and Ethics.

The case shows how someone can look after a place in space without owning it. Each protection binds only those who agreed to it, through a contract or a political promise. A country or company outside those arrangements has no duty under them, and China and Russia, which are building their own lunar plans, are not bound by the Artemis Accords.
for-all-moonkind.why: Accords count was out of date: NASA gave 76 signatories on 28 Sep 2026.

add_sources.t: NASA Celebrates as Artemis Accords Surpasses 75 Signatories, NASA, 28 Sep 2026

change-6.story:
Chang'e 6 was a Chinese robotic mission that collected rock and soil from the far side of the Moon. It landed on 1 June 2024 in the southern part of Apollo Basin. It collected 1,935.3 grams of samples. Its ascent stage carried them back into orbit, and the return capsule reached Inner Mongolia on 25 June. The descent stage stayed behind.

Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, keeps legal authority over that hardware with China, and ownership continues whether an object stays on the Moon or returns to Earth.

Samples raise a harder question. Taking them created no claim to the site, because Article II bars any country from claiming land on the Moon. The treaty does not plainly say how soil from land no country may own comes to be owned once removed, and no court has tested the question.

Governments have answered it in different ways. The United States in 2015, Luxembourg in 2017, the United Arab Emirates in 2019 and Japan in 2021 passed laws saying their companies may own what they extract. Section 10 of the Artemis Accords, a set of principles that countries sign as a political commitment, says extracting resources does not in itself count as a country taking over the body. Luxembourg's own Council of State, which advises on new laws, said it was unclear whether international law allows this. The Moon Agreement of 1979 takes a different line for its few members, calling the Moon's resources the common heritage of mankind and promising an international system to govern mining once it is about to become possible. Even so, Article 6 of that agreement lets its members collect and remove samples for scientific work and keep them at their disposal. China has joined neither the Accords nor the Moon Agreement. Any settlement that means to live off local materials would depend on which of these views other countries come to accept.
change-6.why: Open point stated vaguely; now says who holds which position, using the national laws, Accords Section 10 and Moon Agreement already recorded in the data.

add_sources.t: 51 U.S. Code 51303: Asteroid resource and space resource rights
US, Luxembourg, Emirates and now Japan take the lead to exploit space mining (Atalayar)

janhunen-ceres-megasatellite.story:
This is a design for a large space settlement in high orbit around Ceres, the dwarf planet in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. It was set out by Pekka Janhunen, a Finnish space physicist at the Finnish Meteorological Institute, in a preprint, a paper shared before formal publication, posted in November 2020 and revised in May 2021. He chose Ceres mainly for its nitrogen, which an Earth-like atmosphere requires.

The settlers would not live on Ceres itself, where gravity is very weak. Spinning habitats would be attached by magnetic bearings to one huge disk-shaped frame in orbit, called a megasatellite, and the spin would give the same gravity as Earth. Mirrors would bring in sunlight. Because all the habitats share a frame, people could travel between them without using rocket fuel, and the settlement could keep growing past the living area of Earth. Population density would stay at 500 people per square kilometre, on soil 1.5 metres deep for gardens and trees, deepening to 4 metres if more energy were spent. Each person would account for about 10 million kilograms of material, mostly soil and radiation shielding. The stated aim is a long-lasting world in which all atoms are recycled. A space elevator on Ceres would lift material cheaply, which the author considers feasible because of the low gravity and fast rotation.

The legal problem is what the settlement is made from. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars nations from claiming bodies in space, but it does not say clearly whether digging up and keeping their material counts as claiming them. The United States in 2015, Luxembourg in 2017, the United Arab Emirates in 2019 and Japan in 2021 passed laws saying their companies may own what they extract, and Section 10 of the Artemis Accords, a set of principles countries sign as a political commitment, says extracting does not in itself count as taking over the body. Critics argue that such laws breach the treaty, and no court has tested them. A settlement built entirely of Ceres would depend on the answer. Once built, it would be a spacecraft in orbit under the state that registered it. It remains a paper design.
janhunen-ceres-megasatellite.why: Named the states and instruments behind "some countries" and "others".

add_sources.t: 51 U.S. Code 51303: Asteroid resource and space resource rights
US, Luxembourg, Emirates and now Japan take the lead to exploit space mining (Atalayar)

titan-settlement-proposals.story:
Titan, the largest moon of Saturn, has been proposed as a site for human settlement, more seriously than most places that far from Earth. It has a thick atmosphere of nitrogen and methane, and it is the only known world besides Earth with lakes on its surface, though these hold liquid methane and ethane in place of water, and range from about 1 to 100 kilometres across.

The main advocate is Robert Zubrin, an American aerospace engineer and founder of the Mars Society. In his 1999 book Entering Space he wrote that Saturn is the most valuable of the giant planets, because it is relatively close, has low radiation and has a good system of moons, and that Titan is the best moon for a base. He has called it in certain ways the most hospitable world beyond Earth for colonisation. Stephen Gillett had written about Titan as a home for life in the magazine Analog in 1992.

The supplies are the attraction. Nitrogen could fill out breathing air, as it does on Earth. Water thought to lie beneath the surface could yield oxygen. Nitrogen, methane and ammonia could make fertiliser. Radar studies published in 2008 by Ralph Lorenz's team found hundreds of times more hydrocarbons than Earth's known oil and gas reserves. Power could come from nuclear plants, or from turbines in methane seas where Saturn's pull causes tides of up to a metre. The thick air and weak gravity mean a person in a suit could strap on wings and fly.

The objections are serious. Titan is extremely cold. There is no free oxygen, so burning fuel as on Earth does not work. Gravity is about one-seventh of Earth's, and the long-term effects on bone and muscle, and on children growing up there, are unknown, since all research has been in zero gravity. Children raised there might not be able to adjust to Earth.

No one has gone past proposals on paper. The law would be tested if they did. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars nations from claiming bodies in space, so no settlement could own Titan. The United States, Luxembourg, the United Arab Emirates and Japan have passed laws saying their companies may own what they extract, and the Artemis Accords, a set of principles countries sign as a political commitment, say extraction does not in itself count as claiming a body. Critics argue that such laws breach the treaty, and no court has tested them, so any plan built on Titan's hydrocarbons would face that open question. Settlers would also remain under the law of whichever country registered their craft and base, however long a message took to reach them.
titan-settlement-proposals.why: Named the states and instruments behind "states disagree".

add_sources.t: 51 U.S. Code 51303: Asteroid resource and space resource rights
US, Luxembourg, Emirates and now Japan take the lead to exploit space mining (Atalayar)

lonestar-lunar-data.story:
Lonestar Data Holdings is a company based in St Petersburg, Florida, that wants to run data centres on the Moon. A data centre is a building full of computers that store information for others. Lonestar's chief executive, Christopher Stott, gives two reasons for putting one on the Moon. The first is backup. Undersea cables get cut, and hurricanes, earthquakes and wars can destroy data, while the Moon has almost no weather. The company calls this resilience as a service.

The second reason is legal. More than 100 countries have data sovereignty laws, which restrict where certain data may be stored and processed, often to within the country itself. A company on Earth cannot satisfy all those countries from one place. Lonestar's pitch, as IEEE Spectrum, an engineering magazine, reported it, cites the 1967 Outer Space Treaty's statement that space and the Moon are not subject to national claims. A US spacecraft is under US law, the argument goes, but it could carry a sealed box under British law, or another country's, so one data centre could host many boxes for many customers.

An earlier test was only software, a program running on someone else's computer aboard a previous Intuitive Machines mission, which passed the US Declaration of Independence back and forth with Earth. The next test was called the Freedom Data Center. It weighed 1 kilogram, held 8 terabytes of solid-state storage in a 3D-printed case, and rode on the Athena lander built by the American company Intuitive Machines. It carried data for the Florida state government and the Isle of Man, along with a copy of the video game Starfield and a song from it. SpaceX launched the mission in late February 2025. On 6 March Athena reached the Mons Mouton area, about 5 degrees from the south pole, but it came to rest on its side in a cold crater, 250 metres (820 feet) from its target by the company's figure and more than 400 metres (1,300 feet) by NASA's. The mission was declared over the next day. Lonestar told the TV station FOX 13 that its payload was intact and the only one to survive.

The legal idea has limits that the treaty itself sets. Article VI says each country bears international responsibility for what its companies do in space, and must authorise and keep supervising them. Article VIII says the country that registers a spacecraft keeps legal control over it, even on the Moon. So the data sits inside an object under the authority of some country on Earth, here the United States. The real attraction of the Moon for this purpose is narrower than being beyond all law. A customer may be able to choose which country's law applies to its box by contract, but a court or government can still reach the company, its staff and its offices on Earth. No court is known to have ruled on whether a box on the Moon satisfies a data-location law.
lonestar-lunar-data.why: Freedom was not the first test (IEEE reports an earlier software test on a prior Intuitive Machines mission). Miss distance conflicts: company 250 m, NASA over 400 m.

graham-island-ferdinandea.story:
Graham Island was a volcanic island that rose from the Mediterranean about 30 kilometres south of Sicily in July 1831 and sank again within six months. It is the top of an undersea volcano called Empedocles, which has broken the surface four or five times in recorded history, going back to the 3rd century BC. It is also the best known case of countries rushing to claim land that then disappeared.

The first signs came in late June 1831, when two Royal Navy ships felt an earthquake between Sciacca, a town on the Sicilian coast, and the island of Pantelleria. In early July a smell of sulphur spread through Sciacca. On 12 July a captain from Naples reported smoke rising from the sea, and another ship's captain saw bubbling water. People watching from shore thought it might be a ferry on fire.

By 17 July there was enough land for a Sicilian customs official, Michele Fiorini, to step ashore and plant an oar to claim it for the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, the state then ruling southern Italy and Sicily. The location explains the interest that followed. It sat near the main shipping routes between Sicily and North Africa, closer to Europe than Britain's base at Malta. On 2 August Captain Humphrey Senhouse of the Royal Navy planted the Union Jack and named it after Sir James Graham, head of the Admiralty. King Ferdinand II sent the warship Etna to claim it and name it Ferdinandea. The French geologist Constant Prévost named it Julia, because it was born in July. Spain also declared an interest, which made four rival claimants.

In July and August it reached about 4 square kilometres and 63 metres high, with two small lakes. Tourists came to see it, and nobles reportedly thought of a holiday resort. The diplomats argued. The island was made of tephra, loose volcanic ash and fragments, and once the eruption stopped, the waves cut it down. Officials reported no trace of it by 17 December, and the dispute lapsed unsettled with nothing left to decide.

The summit reappeared briefly in 1863 and now lies about 6 to 8 metres under water, marked on charts as a danger to ships. When it showed signs of activity in 2000 and 2002, Italians placed a flag and a marble plaque on the bank to head off future claims, which indicates that the old quarrel is still remembered. In today's law of the sea, a state's rights over a nearby undersea bank depend on where it lies relative to coasts, so the question would be argued differently. The 1831 episode shows how fast claims form when new land has strategic value, and how quickly loose ash can remove the subject of a dispute.
graham-island-ferdinandea.why: The listed source gives both 6 m and 8 m for the summit depth.

south-talpatti-new-moore.story:
South Talpatti, which India called New Moore and also Purbasha, was a low sandbar in the Bay of Bengal, claimed by both India and Bangladesh. Nobody ever lived on it, and it never stood more than 2 metres above the sea, yet the two countries argued over it for decades.

It formed from silt after the Bhola cyclone of November 1970, in the huge delta where the Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers reach the sea. A US satellite picked it up in 1974 at about 2,500 square metres. It later grew to about 10,000 square metres at low tide. There was speculation that oil and gas lay in the area.

The reason for the quarrel lay in an old border rule. When British India was divided in 1947, the Radcliffe Award set the boundary, and on rivers the border follows the middle of the main channel, a rule known as the thalweg. The sandbar lay only 2 kilometres from the mouth of the Hariabhanga River, which marks the border between the two countries. If the main channel ran to the east of the sandbar, it was on India's side, and if to the west, on Bangladesh's. India said its 1981 survey showed the deep channel on the east, and similar data appeared on British and American charts. Bangladesh said its data showed the main flow on the west. Delta channels also move over time, so it could matter which year was used.

Possession was mostly symbolic. India reportedly raised its flag in 1981 and set up a temporary Border Security Force base, visiting with gunboats. Neither country built anything lasting, because the delta floods every year and reshapes the ground. The stakes were out at sea. The location of the sandbar might have affected where the two countries' sea boundary ran, and with it who controlled the seabed resources offshore.

On 8 October 2009 Bangladesh started arbitration over the wider sea boundary under Annex VII of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the part of that treaty which lets a state take a dispute to a panel of arbitrators chosen for the case. Five arbitrators sat. The Permanent Court of Arbitration, an international body, acted as their registry, meaning their administrative office. In March 2010 Sugata Hazra, an Indian oceanographer at Jadavpur University, reported that the island had disappeared, and named sea level rise, shifting river flows and sinking land as causes. The final award of 7 July 2014, which cannot be appealed, gave Bangladesh 19,467 of about 25,000 square kilometres of disputed sea, and placed the site of the vanished sandbar on India's side. So Bangladesh won most of the water and India won a patch of sea where an island had been.

The case shows that even a useless strip of sand can matter when it might move a boundary at sea. It also shows that the sea rights, once fixed by judges, can outlast the land that started the argument.
south-talpatti-new-moore.why: The case was an UNCLOS Annex VII arbitration; the PCA was only its registry.

add_sources.t: Bay of Bengal Maritime Boundary Arbitration (Bangladesh v. India), PCA Case 2010-16

autopia-saya-de-malha.story:
Autopia was a planned micronation, a small self-declared state, on the Saya de Malha Bank, one of the largest underwater plateaus in the world, northeast of Madagascar and southeast of the Seychelles. The bank covers about 40,800 square kilometres, roughly the size of Belgium by its promoters' description. Parts of it are less than 33 feet deep and covered with sea grass and small coral reefs. The nearest land, tiny Agaléga, is about 300 kilometres away.

The people behind it were the architect Wolf Hilbertz, a professor at the University of Houston, and the marine biologist Thomas Goreau. Hilbertz had patented Biorock, a process that passes a weak electric current through steel frames sunk in seawater, which slowly deposits limestone on them. It creates a surface where corals and shellfish can grow. He hoped to grow buildings this way, with less carbon cost than ordinary concrete, and to create a self-sufficient settlement "that belongs to the residents who live and work there". The name meant the place that builds itself.

The legal attraction was the location. In 2004 Hilbertz said most of the bank lay in international waters, on the high seas, the ocean outside any country's control, governed only by the UN Law of the Sea. The reporter Ian Urbina describes it as hundreds of miles beyond any nation's reach. Wikipedia says that Mauritius administers the whole bank, because part of it lies in Mauritius's exclusive economic zone, the 200-mile belt in which a coastal state controls resources, and that most of the bank is otherwise in international waters. So a builder on the bank might face a claim from Mauritius, depending on the exact spot. Even in open water, the Law of the Sea does not let anyone claim the seabed as a country.

The seabed has its own rules as well. The continental shelf is the seabed over which a coastal state holds rights to resources, and it can reach beyond the 200-mile belt. In April 2011 a UN body endorsed a joint submission by Mauritius and Seychelles for 400,000 square kilometres of such seabed, and on 12 March 2012 the two countries signed a treaty to manage it together. The arrangement concerns the Mascarene Plateau region, and Saya de Malha is part of that plateau. The exact position of a structure would decide whether it stood on seabed covered by the treaty.

On 9 March 1997 the two men sailed three days from Victoria in the Seychelles with solar panels, metal scaffolding and cornerstones. In 2002 they returned in three sailboats with architects, cartographers and marine biologists from several countries. With a cyclone approaching, they built a steel frame five by five metres and two metres high in six days, at 9°12′ south, anchored to the seabed and kept charged by a small battery. Nobody settled there. The plans then stalled for lack of money, so the question of who governed the site was never tested.

The bank later drew another plan. The Italian businessman Samuele Landi, who had been convicted of fraud in Italy and was sentenced in his absence to 14 years, planned to bring barges there from Dubai, far from the reach of extradition. He lived for over a year on a barge called Aisland anchored off Dubai while raising money. On 2 February 2024 a wave broke the barge in two, and Landi and two crew members died, so that plan never reached the bank.
autopia-saya-de-malha.why: Omitted the seabed regime: Mauritius and Seychelles hold and jointly manage extended continental shelf in the Mascarene Plateau region. The treaty text was not retrieved, so the wording leaves the exact overlap open.
autopia-saya-de-malha.mechanism: Open ocean belongs to no state, so the founders expected no legal obstacle on a mid-ocean bank. Any part of the bank within 200 miles of a state's coast falls in that state's exclusive economic zone, where it controls resources, and Mauritius and Seychelles jointly manage a large area of seabed beyond that belt in the same plateau region.

add_sources.t: Mauritius and Seychelles sign Treaty to create world's largest offshore joint management area, Commonwealth, 13 Mar 2012
Maritime Zones (Coordinates of Outer Limits of Extended Continental Shelf in the Mascarene Plateau Region) Regulations 2012, Ecolex

minerva.story:
The Republic of Minerva was an attempt in 1972 to create a new country on the Minerva Reefs, two ring-shaped coral reefs in the South Pacific between Fiji and Tonga, about 270 miles west of Tonga's capital. They were named after the whaling ship Minerva, wrecked there in 1829. The reef surface stands about three feet out of the water at low tide and about four feet under at high tide, so it was a hazard to ships and nobody lived on it.

Its backer was Michael Oliver, a Nevada real estate developer and coin dealer, and a concentration camp survivor. In 1968 he published A New Constitution for a New Country, a model for a state with very limited government paid for voluntarily. He wanted a country with no taxation, welfare, subsidies or economic intervention, where people could do as they pleased if they did not infringe on others' rights. Income would come from fees paid by banks and multinational companies that based themselves there.

He raised money from about 2,000 investors through a body called the Ocean Life Research Foundation, with offices in New York and London. He first tried to buy an island from a government, and no one would sell sovereignty, so the group chose to build its own land. Accounts of the construction differ. Some say barges or a dredging ship brought sand from Australia, while another describes a small party sailing from Fiji in January 1971 with coral wrapped in chicken wire, concrete blocks and rubble. The result was two tiny islands with a stone platform and a flag, a torch on a blue background. The plan was for a resort called Sea City with 30,000 people. No one actually lived there. Minerva dollar coins were struck, including a 35-dollar piece.

A declaration of independence went to neighbouring states and about a hundred nations on 19 January 1972. Morris "Bud" Davis was named provisional president and ran the republic from his living room in Gustine, California.

Neighbours reacted because of what it might mean for them. Tonga had not included the reefs in its 1887 territorial claim, and Fiji's prime minister asked what would stop such people claiming land in Fiji. Australia also objected to a private state in its region. At a conference on 24 February, Australia, New Zealand, Fiji, Nauru, Samoa and the Cook Islands backed a Tongan claim. Tonga proclaimed the reefs and the waters within 12 miles as its own on 15 June. An expedition arrived on 18 June. On 21 June the king, Taufaʻahau Tupou IV, sailed out on the royal yacht with soldiers, a convict work party and a four-piece brass band. He tore down the flag and read a proclamation of sovereignty, and the platform was dismantled within hours. In one account a fight between two of the convicts left one of them dead. In September the South Pacific Forum named Tonga as the only possible owner, without explicitly recognising its title.

Oliver then dismissed Davis and the project collapsed. He went on to back separatists on Abaco in the Bahamas and on Vanuatu, where Papua New Guinean soldiers put down the revolt in 1980. One account also names Australian troops.

The case shows the weakness of the empty-reef idea. International law makes land that no state holds open to the first state that takes it, and a private person is not a state. Once an unclaimed reef became a problem, a neighbour could simply claim it, and the region agreed. A sand pile with no population, army or recognition had nothing to set against that.
minerva.why: Coconut War account has Papua New Guinean soldiers putting down the 1980 revolt; only Pendle names Australian troops.

republic-of-new-afrika.story:
The Republic of New Afrika is a Black nationalist organisation in the United States that seeks an independent country in the Black Belt of the American South, the band of states with historically large African American populations. It also demands reparations from the US government for slavery and the Jim Crow segregation laws, and a vote of African Americans on their citizenship.

Its roots lie in the Black radical movements of the 1960s. Queen Mother Moore and others had drafted a provisional government in 1962, and the Revolutionary Action Movement drew up a nation-within-a-nation programme in 1964. After the Detroit and Newark riots of 1967, activists held a Black Power conference. Then the Malcolm X Society, a Detroit group, called a Black Government Conference in Detroit on 31 March 1968, attended by about 500 people.

It adopted a declaration of independence, a constitution and a provisional government. Robert F. Williams, then living in exile in China after earlier years in Cuba, was chosen as first president, with Gaidi Obadele (Milton Henry) and Betty Shabazz, the widow of Malcolm X, as vice presidents. A delegation met Williams in China in June 1968 and he accepted. He returned to the United States in 1969. The group claimed Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia and South Carolina as "subjugated national territory", and announced a capital on a member's farm in Hinds County, Mississippi. It tried to build institutions, including buying land.

The confrontations that followed decided its fate. Shootouts took place at New Bethel Baptist Church in Detroit in 1969, on the group's first anniversary, and in Jackson, Mississippi, in 1971, in which law-enforcement officers were killed and injured. Members were prosecuted and said they acted in self-defence. The organisation declined in the early 1970s, mainly because of government raids and mass arrests that jailed its leaders.

Its ideas lasted longer. Imari Obadele's books and Nkechi Taifa's Reparations Yes (1993) carried the arguments on. Chokwe Lumumba, elected a vice president in 1971, became a lawyer and was mayor of Jackson from 2013 until his death in 2014. The group still lists officers, though its current activity is not known.

In law, the claim gained no land. A declaration by a provisional government does not move five US states out of the United States, and the federal and state governments treated the group's members as citizens subject to ordinary criminal law. One account describes the state's response as repression of a political movement. Officers were killed in these confrontations, and members were tried for it. No court is known to have ruled on the land claim itself.
republic-of-new-afrika.why: Williams was living in China in 1968 (1966 to 1969), not Cuba. The listed page says Cuba; his own biography gives the dates and the June 1968 meeting.

compacts-of-free-association.story:
The Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands and Palau are three independent countries scattered across the western Pacific that have a special treaty relationship with the United States, called free association. It is a clear example of a way of being a country while handing over one of a country's main jobs.

From 1947 they formed part of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, a UN arrangement run by the US Navy until 1951 and then by the Department of the Interior. The agreement obliged the United States to help the people move towards self-government or independence. Each group chose to become a sovereign state, meaning a self-governing country in law, while keeping close ties to the United States.

Votes in 1983 approved the treaties, known as compacts. These took effect on 21 October 1986 for the Marshall Islands, 3 November 1986 for Micronesia and 1 October 1994 for Palau, whose agreement was signed in 1986 and took eight more years to come into force.

The bargain has two sides. The United States pays guaranteed financial assistance and gives access to some US services. In return it holds full authority over their defence, and foreign forces cannot enter without US permission. The United States is responsible for protecting them, although it may not declare war for them. There are limits on it too. It may not use nuclear, chemical or biological weapons in Palau, and it may not store them in the other two except in an emergency. Citizens may serve in the US armed forces, and many do. In 2008 Micronesia had a higher rate of enlistment per person than any US state.

The agreements have no end date, though the economic terms are renewed from time to time. The 2003 renewal gave Micronesia and the Marshall Islands US$3.5 billion, and the most recent covers 2024 to 2043 under US Public Law 118-42. All three remain independent and in association with the United States.

For someone interested in how small places can become states, this model shows that sovereignty can be divided. A tiny country with few resources can gain recognition as a state, while another state pays for its needs and defends it. The arrangement depends on a larger power willing to pay for that control.
compacts-of-free-association.why: Listed source gives plebiscites in 1983; no source for 1984.

free-territory-of-trieste.story:
The Free Territory of Trieste was meant to be a neutral independent country on the Adriatic Sea between Italy and Yugoslavia, under the direct responsibility of the UN Security Council. It existed in law for seven years and was never run as a country.

Trieste is a port with a mixed Italian and Slovene population and it mattered for trade with Central Europe. At the end of the Second World War, Yugoslav troops took the city, and on 10 June 1945 an agreement at Duino set a dividing line, the Morgan Line, after which they withdrew to their own side. Both Italy and Yugoslavia wanted the port. The planned solution was to give it to neither. In January 1947 Security Council Resolution 16 called for a free state, and the Treaty of Peace with Italy of 10 February 1947 created it, taking effect on 15 September 1947. Its official languages would be Italian and Slovene.

Everything hinged on one post. Its permanent statute would take effect once an international governor was appointed with the approval of the four main powers. The Cold War stopped that. Between October 1947 and March 1948 the Soviet Union rejected 12 successive candidates, and on 20 March 1948 the United States, Britain and France recommended returning the territory to Italy. So no governor was ever appointed and no local government was formed. Its formal status and separate sovereignty were still generally respected, and it took part as a separate state in the Marshall Plan and the related Organisation for European Economic Co-operation.

Instead it stayed split in two along the old line. Zone A, the city and coast, had 222.5 square kilometres and 262,406 people under British and American military rule. Zone B, with 515.5 square kilometres and 71,000 people, was under the Yugoslav army. Each used its own version of the lira, and there were separate postage stamps. For seven years the people of Trieste lived under military governors. The territory still sent a cycling team to a race in Poland in 1950.

On 5 October 1954 the United States, Britain, Italy and Yugoslavia signed the London Memorandum, which ended Allied rule in Zone A. Italy took Zone A and Yugoslavia kept Zone B. The Treaty of Osimo, signed in 1975 and in force from 1977, settled the border between them, so the territory no longer exists. The case shows how much depends on the great powers still agreeing after they have signed. A treaty and a Security Council resolution created this state, and a single unfilled post left it without a government.
free-territory-of-trieste.why: Source says formal status and separate sovereignty were generally respected, not "only in form"; added Marshall Plan and OEEC participation.

new-utopia.story:
New Utopia was a planned tax-free country on concrete platforms over the Misteriosa Bank, an underwater rise in the Caribbean about 115 miles west of the Cayman Islands. It was never built and existed only as an offer to investors, which is how US law reached it.

Howard Turney, who lived in Houston and Tulsa, had become an advocate of human growth hormone and in 1993 opened an anti-ageing clinic in Mexico. Around 1995 he renamed himself Lazarus Long after a long-lived character in Robert Heinlein's novels, called himself Prince Lazarus, and filed a claim to the bank with the United Nations. A UN office has no power to approve such a claim.

The plan drew on Ayn Rand and Heinlein. There would be no income tax, with services paid for by a 20 percent tax on imported consumer goods. Plans included 642 apartments, a casino like Monte Carlo's, and a clinic better than the Mayo Clinic. A website of more than 100 pages drew over 100,000 visits. It offered five-year government bonds, meaning loans to the new country, at 9.5 percent interest, in a $350 million offering, and invited buyers to become charter citizens. It also promised currency returns as high as 200 percent, and showed notes with Long's face.

This is where his location mattered less than his customers. The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), which polices the sale of investments, treats an offer aimed at American investors as subject to US law, wherever the supposed project lies. On 8 April 1999 the SEC filed suit, alleging false statements about construction, the companies involved, the safety of the investment and the SEC's own inquiry. An SEC official said people were making investment decisions based on what they read on a website. Judge Michael Burrage in Tulsa, Oklahoma, issued an emergency order freezing the money, which the Associated Press put near $100,000 at that stage. Long called it a witch-hunt, said he would return the money, and said he wanted people to be able to keep donating to the New Utopia government.

On 20 January 2000 Long accepted a final judgment without contesting it and was barred from further violations. The court ordered him to repay $24,000 plus interest and waived payment because he swore he could not pay, and for the same reason it imposed no civil penalty. The SEC says about $24,000 was raised, while encyclopedia entries claim $100 million.

Long died in April 2012. His daughter, Elizabeth Henderson, announced a revival in 2017, promising completion by 2021, and nothing is known to have come of it. For anyone founding a territory, the case shows that a future country has no shield. Selling bonds in a state that does not exist is a sale of investments by a person who lives somewhere, to buyers who live somewhere, and those places' laws apply.
new-utopia.why: The court, not the SEC, ordered repayment and waived it; no civil penalty was imposed either.

operation-atlantis.story:
Operation Atlantis was an effort to found a new country in the Caribbean, begun in 1968 by Werner Stiefel. Born in Brooklyn in 1921, Stiefel ran the family's Stiefel Medicinal Soap Company, which became the largest privately owned skin-care drug firm in the world. He was inspired by the writer Ayn Rand, especially her novel Atlas Shrugged, and believed postwar America was heading to socialism. He wanted, in his words, to test whether a free capitalist society could exist and flourish.

He set out a plan in three stages. Atlantis I was a motel in Saugerties, New York, near one of his soap plants, where followers would gather and work. Atlantis II was a ship that would sail under the new country's flag in international waters. Atlantis III would be a ship plus an island, a sovereign country as close to US shores as possible. He wrote a book under the pen name Warren K. Stevens to recruit people, and published a monthly bulletin. He paid Spencer Heath MacCallum with a 2 percent share to draft a constitution. Members struck a coin, the deca, holding a decagram of silver, on a soap press. Stiefel kept the project out of the press, so many details are hard to confirm, and how many lived at the motel is not known.

His first choice of land was the Prickly Pear Cays near Anguilla in 1969. He agreed to pay $100,000 and the sale fell through, and one account says the Anguillan government declined to sell.

So he decided to make land. Members spent a year building a 38-foot concrete boat, Atlantis II, under a geodesic dome beside the motel. Launched on the Hudson River in December 1971 at high tide, it capsized as the tide fell and lay sideways in the mud. It was righted, and sailed south, broke a propeller shaft and reached the Bahamas, where a storm destroyed it.

Stiefel bought another ship and went to Silver Shoals, a reef area with water four feet deep at low tide, thought to hold Spanish shipwrecks, and claimed by both Haiti and the Bahamas. He built sea walls and was about to dredge up sand when gunboats ordered the group to leave. Accounts differ on whether they were Haitian or Dominican. One says the captain took them for pirates diving on wrecks. The group was unarmed, and Stiefel, described as appalled by violence, left. He then leased a base on Tortuga, a Haitian island, until officials read the group's newsletter and cancelled the lease. That is a recurring problem for such ventures. Publicity needed to recruit followers also tells the local government what they plan.

An oil rig bound for the Misteriosa Bank between Honduras and Cuba was destroyed by a hurricane, and most members went home. A participant says the group later bought a six-acre island, Hatchet Caye in Belize, and lived there until 2005. There Stiefel sought freeport status from the Belizean government, and in Belize they were ordinary landowners under Belizean law. Stiefel, growing old and tired of working with officials, finally put the island up for sale, which ended Operation Atlantis.

The five years show the order in which the obstacles appear. Nobody will sell sovereignty. Built land in shallow water sits in someone's claimed area. A small navy can remove an unarmed group with no court involved. What a private buyer can actually get is an ordinary island in an ordinary country.
operation-atlantis.why: Added how the project ended, from the listed Wikipedia page.

catalonia-2017.story:
Catalonia is a region of north-eastern Spain, centred on Barcelona, with its own parliament and government. In 2017 it tried to become independent through a referendum that Spain's courts had blocked. It is the best-known recent test of what happens when a wealthy, well-organised region acts against its own country's constitution.

Pro-independence parties had promised a referendum before the 2015 Catalan election. Their coalition won 62 of 135 seats and governed with the support of 10 members from a smaller party. In the earlier parliament the Catalan government had held only a non-binding citizen consultation. The Spanish government called such a vote a breach of the constitution.

On 6 September 2017 the Catalan parliament, under President Carles Puigdemont, approved a referendum law while 52 opposing members boycotted the vote. The next day Spain's Constitutional Court, which rules on whether laws fit the constitution, suspended the law at the request of the Spanish government. The Catalan government went ahead.

The vote took place on 1 October, and National Police and Civil Guard officers used force at polling stations. Yes took 2,044,038 votes, or 90.18 percent, on a turnout of 43.03 percent. The figures are hard to read, because many opponents stayed away. The Catalan government estimated that up to 770,000 votes could not be cast because of the police action, and observers it had invited said the vote fell short of international standards. The court declared the law void on 17 October.

On 27 October the Catalan parliament declared independence by 70 votes to 10, with 2 blank and 55 opposition members refusing to take part. The same day Spain's Senate voted 214 to 47 to use Article 155 of the constitution, which lets the national government take direct control of a region's powers when it breaches its duties. The Spanish government had begun that process on 21 October. No state recognised the declaration, so the declared republic had no outside support.

The criminal courts followed. On 14 October 2019 Spain's Supreme Court, in a unanimous verdict, sentenced nine of twelve accused leaders to prison terms of 9 to 13 years for sedition, four of them also for misuse of public funds. The other three were fined for disobedience, and the charge of rebellion was dismissed. The nine were pardoned in June 2021, though their bans from holding public office stayed in place.

In the 2024 Catalan elections independence parties lost control of the regional government, and an amnesty was passed that year for crimes linked to the referendum. Catalonia remains part of Spain.

The case shows how much the route matters. Scotland held a lawful vote in 2014 because London agreed. Catalonia had a large movement and an existing regional government, and Madrid did not agree, so its vote had no legal effect inside Spain, and other countries left the matter to Spain.
catalonia-2017.why: Added the missing criminal outcome: 2019 convictions and 2021 pardons.

add_sources.t: Trial of Catalonia independence leaders, Wikipedia

moon-agreement.story:
The Moon Agreement is the UN treaty that treats the Moon's resources as belonging to all humanity, and it is the one space treaty most countries have refused. To follow why, it helps to know where it sits. Between 1967 and 1979 UN members concluded five treaties on space, starting with the Outer Space Treaty, which says no country can claim the Moon. That treaty says little about mining. The Moon Agreement was meant to fill the gap.

Argentina, Poland and France raised the idea in the UN's space committee in 1969, and the Soviet Union circulated a draft in May 1971. An American memorandum of that September, since declassified, says the US view was that the Soviet proposal largely repeated the 1967 treaty and was offered as a way to use up committee time, and that the United States would support it. The UN General Assembly adopted the agreement on 5 December 1979, and it took effect on 11 July 1984.

The core is Article 11. It repeats that no one can claim the Moon, and says natural resources in place, meaning still in the ground, cannot become anyone's property. Collecting samples for science is allowed separately by Article 6. Article 11 then calls the Moon's resources the common heritage of mankind, and commits members to set up an international system to govern mining once mining is about to become possible. That system is meant to manage the resources sensibly and share the benefits equitably, with special consideration for countries that contributed to exploring the Moon. The same model is used for the deep seabed, where the International Seabed Authority manages mining under the Law of the Sea. For someone planning a settlement or a mine, the difference is large. Under the 1967 treaty a company might hope to keep what it digs up. Under this one, an international body would have a say and a share.

That is the reason for most of the opposition. In the United States, campaigners from the L5 Society, a group of space settlement enthusiasts, fought the treaty in 1979 and 1980, arguing that common heritage would stifle development. The United States and the Soviet Union did not join, and neither has any other leading space power. The US later issued an executive order stating that it rejects the agreement, on the grounds that legal uncertainty was discouraging companies.

A treaty binds only the countries that join it. The UN treaty database lists 17 members, including Australia, Austria, Belgium, Chile, Mexico, the Netherlands and Pakistan. France, Guatemala, India and Romania signed but never ratified. Saudi Arabia joined on 18 July 2012, signed the US-led Artemis Accords on 14 July 2022, and notified the UN on 5 January 2023 that it was leaving, the first withdrawal from any of the five space treaties. Its exit took effect on 5 January 2024. For All Moonkind and others suggested it wanted freedom to mine under national law.

The treaty remains in force for its members, and the international mining system has never been set up. Mining itself has not yet begun, so the promise in Article 11 has not yet come due.
moon-agreement.why: Sample collection is in Article 6, not Article 11; added that Article 11 bars property in resources "in place".

add_sources.t: Moon Agreement, full text, UN Office for Outer Space Affairs
